stories.headline: 2nd Circuit deals blow to Manhattan DA, breathes new life into Trump's hush money appeal
stories.note: A federal appeals court gave Trump a fresh shot at moving his hush money case out of Alvin Bragg's state court.
body: President Trump scored a win at the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, which revived his effort to move his New York hush money case out of state court and into the federal system.

A three-judge panel ruled that the late U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein erred in August when he rejected Trump's second transfer request. The panel said a federal official can still seek removal after a conviction, and that Trump had shown good cause to try again. A full opinion is still to come.

Trump was convicted in May 2024 on 34 counts of falsifying business records tied to a $130,000 payment to Stormy Daniels, and received an unconditional discharge in January 2025. His lawyers argue the Supreme Court's 2024 immunity ruling changed the landscape because prosecutors used evidence of official presidential acts at trial.
Manhattan prosecutors had urged the court to keep Hellerstein's ruling, accusing Trump of "strategic delay" and arguing the payoff had nothing to do with his official duties.

The question now goes to U.S. District Judge Lewis J. Liman, and the panel asked New York courts to pause proceedings meanwhile. Even if the case moves, the charges remain state offenses that a presidential pardon can't reach.
Why it matters: The ruling reopens a real path to wiping out Alvin Bragg's signature conviction of Trump, a major setback for the Democratic prosecutor.

stories.headline: Newsom shredded for ‘hypocritical’ claim Trump 'sells' pardons after moving to spare 548 death row inmates
stories.note: Newsom's pardon attack on Trump is backfiring as critics point to his own mass clemency for death row inmates.
body: California Gov. Gavin Newsom is facing a wave of criticism after calling for limits on presidential pardon powers just days after he moved to commute the death sentences of 548 inmates to life without parole.
In a video defending his decision, Newsom accused President Trump of turning mercy into a business, saying, "Donald Trump doesn't oppose mercy. He sells it."

Critics pounced on the contrast. Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., mocked the governor on X as an arsonist calling for a ban on fire. Trump, appearing at the Justice Department with Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and relatives of victims, said Newsom had robbed families of closure and vowed to seek the death penalty for child murderers.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier led 14 attorneys general in condemning the plan, and California prosecutors and victims' relatives have asked the state Supreme Court to halt it. California voters rejected abolishing the death penalty in 2012 and 2016.
Newsom's office did not respond to Fox News Digital. Some critics suggest the move is aimed at a 2028 presidential run, where he's seen as a leading Democratic contender.
Why it matters: Newsom is handing Republicans a ready-made soft-on-crime attack as he positions himself for the Democratic nomination.

stories.headline: Pritzker accused of turning education tax credit into partisan fight by opting out of program: 'Sad to see'
stories.note: Pritzker is taking heat for keeping Illinois families out of a school-choice tax credit program.
body: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker announced Tuesday that his state won't opt into the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program created under President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, drawing fire from parents and school-choice advocates.

The program gives a federal tax credit for donations of up to $1,700 to scholarship-granting organizations, which help families with costs like private school tuition, tutoring and textbooks, including for public school students.

Pritzker called it a voucher scheme that would siphon money from public schools. Teach Coalition CEO Sydney Altfield countered that it doesn't take a dollar from public schools and said Illinois residents can still claim the credit, meaning an estimated $2 billion or more in scholarship money could flow out of state.

Altfield called it "really sad to see" kids caught in partisan politics. Democratic governors Jared Polis of Colorado, Kathy Hochul of New York and Michelle Lujan Grisham of New Mexico have opted in, while GOP legislatures in Kansas, Kentucky and North Carolina overrode Democratic governors' vetoes to join.
Why it matters: Pritzker, a possible 2028 Democratic contender, is now on record blocking scholarship help for families even as some fellow Democrats embrace the GOP's school-choice program.

stories.headline: Socialists on blast for pledging to weed money out of politics but accepting business execs' checks anyway
stories.note: Democratic socialists are being called out for taking executive cash despite anti-big-money pledges.
body: Democratic Socialists who campaign against corporate influence are facing hypocrisy charges after a review of Federal Election Commission filings showed they took money from corporate executives and PACs.

The filings, first flagged by the nonprofit 1792 Exchange and reviewed by Fox News Digital, show Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., received $10,600 from an L3Harris defense executive despite writing a 2025 op-ed criticizing lawmakers who profit from the defense industry.

Reps.-elect Donavan McKinney of Michigan and Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York pledged to reject corporate PAC money but still took cash from PACs and executives. The investigation found 24 executives gave a combined $675,300 to DSA-endorsed candidates or allied progressive PACs over two cycles.
Rep.-elect Jerry Carl, R-Ala., said if they're taking the money, they should at least admit it. The records do not show any executive sought or received favors in return.
None of the DSA members, the DSA itself or the progressive PACs responded to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.
Why it matters: The far-left wing driving Democrats' agenda is being exposed for preaching against big money while quietly cashing executives' checks.

stories.headline: DOJ lawyers ordered to swarm 'frivolous' 97,000-lawsuit wave from ICE detainees
stories.note: The Trump DOJ is throwing more lawyers at a flood of detainee lawsuits to keep deportations moving.
body: Attorney General Todd Blanche is pulling civil litigators from across the Justice Department into the fight against a flood of habeas corpus petitions from detained illegal immigrants.

In a three-page memo issued Tuesday, Blanche called the lawsuits "frivolous" and an effort to thwart President Trump's promise to keep Americans safe. The department has faced about 97,000 such petitions since January 2025, nearly 10,000 of them since October, compared with a few hundred in a typical year.

Lawyers from the Antitrust, Civil Rights, Civil, and Environment and Natural Resources divisions, plus senior leadership offices, are being tapped. Division leaders have 30 days to submit an aggressive appellate strategy and send attorneys to high-volume districts.

The surge followed the administration's move to deny bond hearings to migrants arrested inside the country. Immigration attorneys pushed back, with one calling Blanche's description of some judges as corrupt "slander." The Supreme Court is set to hear a challenge to the detention policy in early 2027.
Why it matters: With nearly 1.2 million illegal immigrants removed so far, the DOJ is signaling it won't let a litigation wave slow the deportation agenda.

stories.headline: Federal grand jury hears evidence in Ilhan Omar investigation, as court records use 3 versions of her name
stories.note: The federal case around Rep. Omar is advancing to a grand jury, keeping the scandal hanging over House Democrats.
body: A federal grand jury in Minnesota is hearing evidence in the investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., sources told Fox News. Prosecutors call it a pre-indictment investigation, and no charges have been filed.

Sources say there are at least two active probes: one into alleged immigration fraud, which reportedly began under President Obama, and another into Omar's finances, opened under President Biden. Omar has repeatedly denied wrongdoing.

Newly unsealed records refer to her by three versions of her name, including Ilhan Nur Said Elmi. Investigators are examining whether she used a false name or birthdate to obtain citizenship. Her birth year was listed as 1981 in many sources before her office had it corrected to 1982 in 2019, a difference that bears on whether she qualified for derivative citizenship as a minor.
Prosecutors described the probe as covering possible violations from 1980 to the present. The records were partially unsealed by Chief Judge James Boasberg after news organizations sought access.
Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., said that where there's "smoke" there may be fire, noting a judge had to find probable cause for the search.
Why it matters: A grand jury hearing evidence is a serious escalation, keeping a cloud over one of the most prominent members of the Democrats' progressive Squad.

stories.headline: Troubling side effects of Walz’s signature legislation triggering local outrage as he heads for the exit
stories.note: Walz is leaving office amid local backlash over the side effects of his signature law.
body: Minnesota's paid family and medical leave law, signed by outgoing Democratic Gov. Tim Walz, is straining local government services less than a year after taking effect.

The law lets workers take up to 12 weeks a year with partial pay for a newborn or sick relative, and up to 12 more for their own serious illness. The Minnesota Star Tribune reported nearly one in four Minneapolis city employees has used it.

A viral clip from an October Minneapolis City Council budget meeting showed an emergency communications official saying 41% of her 911 staff were out on the program. The resulting overtime is contributing to a proposed $1.5 million budget increase. She also confirmed new hires can take the leave right away and then quit.

Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., called it "the definition of waste and abuse." Bill Glahn of the Center of the American Experiment said his group had warned for years that workers would use the program as written, leading to tax hikes to pay for both the benefit and replacement staff.
Why it matters: Walz's signature achievement is becoming a cautionary tale about Democratic big-government programs as he leaves office.
